text:
Instructor

 John Paul Helveston

This course builds a foundation in how to use AI agents to build a variety of artifacts, such as websites, writing, images, animations, music, PDFs, data visualizations, and slide decks. Students will develop the professional engineering skills — version control with Git and GitHub, testing, continuous integration, and deployment with GitHub Pages — that make agentic work sustainable and reliable. Each week pairs a concept taught in class with a new artifact to build, along with new skills for working with agents, including managing context and tokens, writing agent skills, calling other AI models through APIs, and keeping data separate from the artifacts it ends up in. The course ends with an individual final project of students’ own design. Students will leave with transferable workflow skills, the judgment to know when and how to verify AI output, and the ability to use AI tools to teach themselves new domains to tackle harder problems.
Short Bulletin Description: AI workflows to accurately and responsibly build software, media, documents, and data visualizations across domains. AI strengths/weaknesses, context management, and token efficiency.



Students should have completed at least one introductory programming course (e.g., CSCI 1012, EMSE 4571, or equivalent). While students will not hand-type much code in this course, they do need to be able to read code, follow code logic, and notice when something is wrong. Most of the code covered in class will be in Python or web languages (HTML, CSS, and JavaScript), though students do no need prior experience with web languages.

title: Syllabus
text:
Agent → code → artifact
From Week 5 on, we build everything the same way. The agent writes the code, you run the code, and the code builds the artifact. We don’t ask the AI to hand us the finished website, image, or PDF directly. Building through code gives you something you can reproduce, it uses far fewer tokens, and it gives you control when you want to change something. Instead of re-prompting the AI to start over, you just change a few lines of code (either yourself, or with the agent’s help).

title: Syllabus
text:
You control Git
Git is how you know what an agent changed. In this class you always control Git yourself. We never let the agent make commits for you. Review what the agent changed (e.g., the diff in GitHub Desktop), check that it works, and then commit it yourself with a message that says what changed.

title: Syllabus
text:
Participation & Attendance
Attendance will be taken and will be part of your participation grade. In-person attendance is critical as we will spend most of class building things together. You should plan to attend class in person each week.
There will be no option for remote attendance (e.g. zoom), and class sessions will not be recorded. If you have any questions or need special accommodations, send the teaching team a message on slack and we can discuss. If you must miss class for an excused absence (e.g. medical issue), please message Professor Helveston and get notes from your fellow classmates.
Multiple absences, inappropriate or unprofessional behavior during class (such as monopolizing discussions or being rude or disruptive), not participating in classroom exercises, and not being prepared for class will result in a poor score for attendance and participation.

title: Syllabus
text:
Quizzes
There will be 13 short quizzes, one at the start of every class from Week 2 on (check the schedule). Quizzes are handwritten on paper, with no devices or notes. They are conceptual: they test whether you understand the ideas from the previous week (what a token is, what a commit records, why an agent shouldn’t retype your data), not whether you can write code from memory.
Quizzes are short (10 minutes) and are designed to test for fluency and to demonstrate where additional study is needed. Your lowest two are dropped. If you do poorly on one or two, use that as feedback on where you need additional improvement.
The best way to ensure you do well on quizzes is to be active in class and complete your builds on time.
Make up quizzes are not available. If you arrive late, you can take the quiz in the remaining time left, but you will not be given additional time. Make ups will only be allowed for excused absences that are discussed and agreed upon with the professor prior to class. If you contact the professor after class for a make up, it will not be granted unless a true emergency prevented you from attending class that could not have been communicated earlier.

Why quiz at all? Research shows that giving small quizzes throughout a class can dramatically help with retention. It’s a phenomenon known as the “retrieval effect” - basically, you have to practice remembering things, otherwise your brain won’t remember them. The phenomenon and research on it is explained in detail in the book “Make It Stick: The Science of Successful Learning,” by Brown, Roediger, and McDaniel.

title: Syllabus
text:
Builds
Each week from Week 1 through Week 13 there is a take-home build: you use that week’s concept to make something on your own. There are 13 builds in total, and your lowest build score is dropped.
Every build is submitted in its own folder (build1, build2, etc.) in your course repo, a private GitHub repo that the teaching team creates for each of you in the class GitHub organization. The repo name is your GW netID, so it will be viewable at https://github.com/bwai-f27/netID, replacing netID with your GW netID. Each build folder includes:

the build itself.
the transcript of your work with the AI (your prompts, its responses, and your iterations), saved as transcript.md
from Build 5 on, a short token usage report (we’ll learn how to measure this in Week 5).

Builds are graded on a 0 / 0.5 / 1 scale using the build rubric. Your grades and feedback come back to you in the feedback folder of the same repo. You may discuss approaches with your classmates, but every build is your own work.

title: Syllabus
text:
Final Project
The final project is individual: everyone builds their own project of their own design, using the workflow and the kinds of things we’ve built during the semester. We introduce the project in Week 8 so you have time to think about it. Both deliverables are submitted in the project folder of your course repo:

Proposal (due Oct 27). A short, high-level description of what you want to build. It’s graded for completion (1 if you submit it, 0 if you don’t). Its purpose is to get you feedback early on whether your idea is a good one and whether it’s well scoped.
Final submission (due Dec 8). A link to the GitHub repository with your project and all of its source files, your transcripts, a token usage report, and a 5-minute video about your project posted to YouTube. In Week 15 we’ll learn to build slide decks, which you can use in your video if you wish. Graded 0 / 0.5 / 1 using the final project rubric.

The teaching team will grade the projects before the final exam, and we’ll start the exam period by showcasing a few of them. View the final project overview page for more details.

title: Syllabus
text:
How Assignments Are Graded
Most grading will be done by an AI agent, with some caveats.

Quizzes and the final exam will be graded by an AI agent using a combination of tools like OCR for handwriting recognition. Answers to these questions are relatively objective and follow a strict rubric, so AI grading here means simply applying the rubric to those responses, which is quite accurate. For a few subjective questions the rubric will be flagged for human review. Feedback will include the correct answer, which can be compared by the students to their responses.
Builds will be mostly graded by an AI agent. For each build, the agent will read your repository, your transcript, and your token report, check your work against the rubric below, and draft a score and feedback. The teaching team will review those drafts and make the final call.
Final projects will be graded by a combination of an AI agent and the teaching team. Agents will be used to draft summaries of what was submitted by each student in an organized way such that the teaching team can efficiently review the submissions. The team will also watch and rank the 5-minute video recordings of each project to verify the agents’ decisions and override those decisions where appropriate.

If you think a grade is wrong, ask for a re-grade and the teaching team will review it.

title: Syllabus
text:
Rounding
Final grades will NOT be rounded. This is because wherever the line is drawn, there will always be students just below or just above, and rounding will only move that bar and create another group of students who are just below and just above. Rounding does not eliminate the issue but rather just shifts it to another group of students. This is why we draw the lines before the course starts - to ensure a fair and transparent system for everyone, that way you don’t have to shoot for a moving bar. To be clear, this means we will not modify or round your final score, even if you’re very close to a different letter grade (e.g., a 93.98 is an “A-” and will not be rounded up to an “A”).
Rather than round, we grade generously throughout the semester. For example, if you give a quiz your best shot and completely fail it, you will likely get a 50% instead of a 0%. The 50% is for trying as learning still happens when you try regardless if you get the question correct (0s are reserved for those who simply don’t attempt it).

title: Syllabus
text:
An AI coding agent (about $20/month)
We will use and teach Claude Code in class, which requires at least a Claude Pro subscription (about $20/month). You’re welcome to use an alternative, such as Gemini CLI (free with a Google account) or Codex (needs a paid ChatGPT plan). The underlying skills transfer, but in-class instruction and course materials assume Claude Code, so you’re on your own for translating anything tool-specific.
Why a subscription and not the API? Agents burn through a lot of tokens. Paying per token through an API would cost far more than a flat monthly subscription.

title: Syllabus
text:
An image-generation API key (Week 7 on)
We don’t use Claude to make images. Starting in Week 7, your agent will call Google’s image model (Nano Banana) through the Gemini API. This is paid per image, but if you’re careful it should only add up to a few dollars over the semester. We’ll set up API keys in class, including how to keep them secret (never in your code, never in a commit).

Late Policy
Each student is allowed 3 late build submissions - use them however you want, no questions asked. These are meant to cover illness, family emergencies, and religious holidays. For each one of these, you can submit a build up to 3 days beyond the deadline and still recieve full credit.
Beyond those, all other assignments are due by 11:59pm on the assigned due date unless specified otherwise. Assignments submitted beyond 24 hours past the deadline will not be graded and will be assigned a 0. The final project cannot use a late submission, since the teaching team needs time to grade the projects before the final exam.
If you need a special accommodation such as due to an illness, family emergency, or religious holidays, contact the instructor ahead of time.

title: Syllabus
text:
Use of AI
Using AI in this course is required. It’s the core skill being taught. Every build and the final project must be made with AI, and you must submit your transcripts.
Now, LLMs are pretty good, but sometimes they suck. Don’t blindly trust them - they will betray you. You are fully responsible for everything you submit, so read what the agent produces, run it, look at the result, and fix it when it’s wrong. That’s what the verification loops we learn in Week 8 are for.
This is what we mean when we say “don’t be AI lazy.” It’s easy to hand the reigns of your builds to AI and just submit it. But you’ll learn nothing. This class is designed to give you plenty of opportunities to engage with the AI tools we will be covering, and to verify their outputs. Just because the AI can write your code for you doens’t mean the AI is in charge or correct. You have to harness it. Your work needs to be correct and good, not slop.
There are three places where AI is not allowed, each for a reason:

Week 1 and Build 1 (Git by hand). You can’t supervise an agent that changes your files until you understand version control yourself.
Git, all semester. The agent never makes commits for you (see You control Git). Your commits are how you show that you reviewed what the agent did.
Quizzes and the final exam. These are handwritten, with no devices, because they test what you understand.

Your transcripts are read by Claude (for grading) and by the teaching team, and are used only for grading this course. Before you submit, remove API keys, passwords, and any personal information from them.
We don’t use AI-detection software (it’s unreliable). The record of your work is your transcript and your Git history. We also use AI ourselves, to help prepare course materials and to draft build grades and feedback, and we review everything before you see it.
Throughout the course we’ll talk about where AI fails, what it costs (in money and energy), copyright and authorship, and when not to use it.

Curious how LLMs actually work? That’s Week 2. If you want a head start, check out this article, which provides a simplified description of how they work (which itself is still quite complicated).

title: Syllabus
text:
Cheating
Cheating results in a penalty on the first offense, and failing the course on the second offense. Cheating on builds and the final project can include:

Submitting someone else’s work or transcript as your own, in any amount.
Editing a transcript to hide or fake what happened. (Removing secrets and personal information is fine and expected.)
Providing your builds or transcripts to anyone else in the class.
Putting solutions to course assignments online.
Getting someone else to do the assignment for you.

Cheating on quizzes or the final exam can include:

Referring to any external resources while completing it (phones, notes, AI tools, etc.).
Copying part of an answer off of another student’s paper, even if it is very small.
Using solutions provided by students who previously took the course.


Penalties
Violations will be reported to the Office of Student Rights & Responsibilities. Penalties are decided by the course instructors, and can vary based on the severity of the offense. Possible penalties include:

Receiving a 0 on the assignment/quiz in question.
Receiving a full letter grade deduction in the course.
Automatically failing the course.

Depending on the student’s prior academic history, violations may also be accompanied by a letter to the Dean of Student Affairs, again at the instructors’ discretion. This can lead to university-level penalties, such as being suspended or expelled.


Grace Period
College is a time when you do a lot of learning. Sometimes, you might make bad decisions or mistakes. The most important thing for you to do is to learn from your mistakes, to constantly grow, and become a better person.
Sometimes, students panic and copy someone else’s work right before the deadline, then regret what they did afterwards. Therefore, you may rescind any build submission for up to 24 hours after the deadline with no questions asked. Simply message the course instructors asking to delete the submission in question, and we will do so. Deleted submissions will not be graded. However, it will always be better to get a 0 (or partial credit) on an assignment than to get a cheating violation!

title: Syllabus
text:
Children in class


I applaud all of you who attend school with children! It is difficult to balance academic, work, and family commitments, and I want you to succeed. Here are my policies regarding children in class:

All breastfeeding babies are welcome in class as often as necessary.
Non-nursing babies and older children are welcome whenever alternate arrangements cannot be made. As a parent of young children, I understand that babysitters fall through, partners have conflicting schedules, children get sick, and other issues arise that leave parents with few other options.
In cases where children come to class, I invite parents/caregivers to sit close to the door so as to more easily excuse yourself to attend to your child’s needs. Non-parents in the class: please reserve seats near the door for your parenting classmates.
All students are expected to join with me in creating a welcoming environment that is respectful of your classmates who bring children to class.
Likewise, parents that bring children to class are expected to excuse themselves to attend to their child’s needs if they become disruptive.

I understand that sleep deprivation and exhaustion are among the most difficult aspects of parenting young children. The struggle of balancing school, work, childcare, and school is tiring, and I will do my best to accommodate any such issues while maintaining the same high expectations for all students enrolled in the class. Please do not hesitate to contact me with any questions or concerns.

Lauren’s Promise


I will listen and believe you if someone is threatening you.
Lauren McCluskey, a 21-year-old honors student athlete, was murdered on October 22, 2018 by a man she briefly dated on the University of Utah campus. We must all take action to ensure that this never happens again.
If you are in immediate danger, call 911 or GWU police at 202-994-6111 (GWPD).
If you are experiencing sexual assault, domestic violence, or stalking, if you report it to me I will listen and connect you to resources or call GWU’s Counseling and Psychological Services (202-994-5300).
Any form of sexual harassment or violence will not be excused or tolerated at GWU. GWU has instituted procedures to respond to violations of these laws and standards, programs aimed at the prevention of such conduct, and intervention on behalf of the victims. GWU Police officers will treat victims of sexual assault, domestic violence, and stalking with respect and dignity. Advocates on campus and in the community can help with victims’ physical and emotional health, reporting options, and academic concerns.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
section: Do I have to pay for Claude Pro?
text:
Do I have to pay for Claude Pro?
To use Claude Code, yes: a free Claude account isn’t enough. But check Slack before you pay in case we get institutional access. If you’d rather not pay, Gemini CLI is free with a Google account. See AI Tools and Cost for details, and let me know if the cost is a barrier for you.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
section: Can I use Codex, Gemini CLI, or some other agent instead of Claude Code?
text:
Can I use Codex, Gemini CLI, or some other agent instead of Claude Code?
Yes. The underlying skills transfer. Just know that in-class instruction, troubleshooting help, and the course materials assume Claude Code, so you’re on your own for translating anything tool-specific.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
section: I hit my usage limit. What do I do?
text:
I hit my usage limit. What do I do?
Subscriptions have usage limits that reset after a while, so you can wait it out. But the better fix is to use fewer tokens in the first place, which is a big part of what we learn in Week 5:

Start a fresh session (or use /clear) when you switch to a new task instead of running one giant conversation all week.
Plan before you build, so the agent doesn’t write (and rewrite) things you didn’t want.
Have the agent write code that builds your artifact instead of asking it to produce the artifact directly. Small changes to code are much cheaper than regenerating the whole thing.

And start your builds early, so a usage limit doesn’t hit you the night before a deadline.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
section: Why can’t I let the agent make commits for me?
text:
Why can’t I let the agent make commits for me?
Because Git is how you know what the agent changed. When you review the changes in GitHub Desktop and commit them yourself, you’re checking the agent’s work. If the agent commits for you, nobody checked. See You control Git in the syllabus.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
section: The agent says it’s done, but it doesn’t work
text:
The agent says it’s done, but it doesn’t work
This happens all the time. Agents are confident, and they’re often wrong. Run the code yourself and look at the result. Then tell the agent exactly what’s wrong: paste the error message, or describe what you see versus what you expected. “It doesn’t work” is much less helpful than “the menu page renders but none of the images show up.”
Only commit once you’ve checked that it actually works.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
section: The agent broke something that used to work
text:
The agent broke something that used to work
This is why we commit often. In GitHub Desktop, the Changes tab shows you everything that changed since your last commit, so you can see exactly what the agent touched. If the changes are a mess, right-click and choose Discard changes to go back to your last commit, then start a fresh session and try again with a clearer request. If the problem is in something you already committed, the History tab shows each commit, and you can revert one from there.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
section: I accidentally committed my API key!
text:
I accidentally committed my API key!
Don’t panic, but act fast. Treat the key as compromised. Deleting it in a new commit doesn’t remove it from your Git history, and anything pushed to GitHub may already have been seen.

Delete (revoke) the key wherever you created it, and make a new one.
Put the new key in a .env file, and make sure .env is listed in your .gitignore so Git never tracks it.
Let me know, and we’ll clean up the repo together.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
section: Why do we build things through code instead of just asking the AI for them?
text:
Why do we build things through code instead of just asking the AI for them?
Code gives you something you can reproduce, it uses far fewer tokens, and it gives you control. If you want to change one thing, you change one line of code instead of re-rolling the whole thing and hoping. See Agent → code → artifact in the syllabus.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
section: Can I use AI on the quizzes or the final exam?
text:
Can I use AI on the quizzes or the final exam?
No. Quizzes and the final exam are handwritten, with no devices or notes, because they test what you understand.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
section: It says claude: command not found (or uv: command not found)
text:
It says claude: command not found (or uv: command not found)
Close your terminal and open a new one (in Positron, use the trash icon on the terminal panel, then Terminal > New Terminal). The installer teaches your computer where the program lives, and only a freshly opened terminal knows about it. That fixes it nine times out of ten. If it still doesn’t work, go back through the steps on the Software page.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
section: Positron won’t let me save my file
text:
Positron won’t let me save my file
Most often times this occurs for one of two reasons:

You may have double-clicked a file instead of opening the folder it lives in. Positron then isn’t “looking” at that folder, and neither is your agent. Close it, then use File › Open Folder… and choose the folder itself.
If you’re on a windows computer, you may have opened the file from inside a zip file. As a result, you can’t save anything because everything is still zipped up. Go back and extract the files from the zip first (right-click the zip and choose “extract all”), then open the extracted folder in Positron.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
section: My Quarto document can’t find a Python package
text:
My Quarto document can’t find a Python package
If you see an error like ModuleNotFoundError: No module named ... when rendering, Quarto probably isn’t using your project’s Python. Check that:

The package is installed in the project (uv add package-name).
ipykernel is installed in the project (uv add ipykernel).
You’re rendering through uv: uv run quarto render.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
section: My site works on my computer but not on GitHub Pages
text:
My site works on my computer but not on GitHub Pages
A few common culprits:

GitHub Pages isn’t turned on for the repo, or it’s pointed at the wrong branch or folder (check Settings › Pages on GitHub).
There’s no index.html where GitHub Pages expects it.
A file name doesn’t match its link exactly. GitHub Pages is case-sensitive, so Photo.png and photo.png are different files, even if your computer treats them the same.
You haven’t pushed your latest commits. Check GitHub Desktop.

title: EMSE 4197: Build with AIFall 2027
text:
EMSE 4197: Build with AIFall 2027
Department: Engineering Management and Systems Engineering @ GWU
Credits: 3
Description:
This course builds a foundation in how to use AI agents to build a variety of artifacts, such as websites, writing, images, animations, music, PDFs, data visualizations, and slide decks. Students will develop the professional engineering skills — version control with Git and GitHub, testing, continuous integration, and deployment with GitHub Pages — that make agentic work sustainable and reliable. Each week pairs a concept taught in class with a new artifact to build, along with new skills for working with agents, including managing context and tokens, writing agent skills, calling other AI models through APIs, and keeping data separate from the artifacts it ends up in. The course ends with an individual final project of students’ own design. Students will leave with transferable workflow skills, the judgment to know when and how to verify AI output, and the ability to use AI tools to teach themselves new domains to tackle harder problems.
Learning Objectives:
Having successfully completed this course, students will be able to:

Explain, in non-technical terms, how AI models work (including tokens and context) and why that leads to their strengths, weaknesses, and failure modes.
Direct AI agents to build a wide range of artifacts, such as websites, writing, images, animations, documents, data visualizations, and slide decks, for a defined goal.
Apply a reliable, reproducible workflow for agentic work: version control with Git and GitHub, building artifacts through code, and managing context, tokens, and cost efficiently.
Verify AI output for accuracy, quality, and fitness for purpose, and correct or reject it when it falls short.
Use AI responsibly, by protecting secrets and private data, respecting attribution and authorship, and disclosing AI use.

Prerequisites:
Students should have completed at least one introductory programming course (e.g., CSCI 1012, EMSE 4571, or equivalent). While students will not hand-type much code in this course, they do need to be able to read code, follow code logic, and notice when something is wrong. Most of the code covered in class will be in Python or web languages (HTML, CSS, and JavaScript), though students do no need prior experience with web languages.
Course developer: This course was developed by John Paul Helveston.

Install the core class software

Sign up for Slack. You should have been sent a link to join in the course intro email. If not, email Professor Helveston for an invite link. I recommend using your @gwu.edu email to sign up, but if you use another email for another Slack then use that.
Install the Slack app on your phone and Turn notifications on!. I’ll send all course communication via Slack, so please make sure your notifications are on so you don’t miss anything.
Install Positron, the code editor we’ll use all semester: download it here and follow the install instructions for your OS. Positron is a free editor from Posit (the company behind RStudio), and it’s where we’ll work with Python, Quarto, and Claude Code together in one place.
Download and install Quarto. We’ll use Quarto to build websites, documents, and slides.
Install uv, the tool we’ll use to install and run Python. Open Positron, choose Terminal > New Terminal from the menu bar, then paste the line for your computer into the terminal and press Enter.
macOS
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
Windows
powershell -ExecutionPolicy ByPass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"
Then close that terminal (the trash icon on the terminal panel), open a new one, and run uv python install to install Python. If you see command not found, opening a fresh terminal is usually the fix. See the uv docs if you get stuck.
Download and install GitHub Desktop. All of our Git work in this class happens in GitHub Desktop, not the terminal.
Create your GitHub account: If you do not yet have a GitHub account, you’ll need to create one. Choose a user name that you like, recognizing that this will be viewed by many in the professional world (Professor Helveston’s is jhelvy), and use a personal email address that will follow you after leaving GW (I recommend not using your GW email as it eventually expires). Then open GitHub Desktop and sign in with that account.

title: Software & Setup
text:
Install an agentic CLI tool
We start using AI coding agents in Week 3, so you’ll need one installed. I will use and teach Claude Code in class as the primary agentic tool I recommend, though you are welcome to use an alternative such as Google Gemini CLI.

Installing Claude Code
You install Claude Code from inside Positron. Work through these five steps before the first day of class. You will need macOS 13 or newer, or Windows 10 or newer.






Tip



Below are my suggested installation steps. If you have any difficulty, look over Anthropic’s Quickstart guide. If you’re still stuck, we can sort it out with you before or after class.



Step 1: Get a Claude subscription
If you do not already have one, sign up now (but check Slack first in case we have institutional access). You’ll need at least a Claude Pro subscription to use Claude Code – a free account isn’t sufficient.


Step 2: Open a terminal inside Positron
Open Positron, then from the menu bar, choose Terminal > New Terminal. A panel opens along the bottom of the window. Everything below happens in that panel, so you never need to leave Positron.


Step 3: Run the installer
Paste the line for your computer into the terminal, then press Enter.
macOS
curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash
Windows
irm https://claude.ai/install.ps1 | iex


Step 4: Close that terminal, then open a new one
Use the trash icon on the terminal panel, then Terminal > New Terminal again. This step matters: the installer teaches your computer where claude lives, and only a freshly opened terminal knows about it.
To check that it worked, type claude --version and press Enter. You should see a version number such as 2.1.211 (Claude Code). If you instead see command not found, opening a new terminal is what fixes it nine times out of ten.


Step 5: Log in
Type claude and press Enter. A browser window opens: sign in with the Claude account you paid for in step 1. You only do this once.

title: Software & Setup
text:
Alternatives to Claude Code
Claude Code is not the only agent that works this way. Both of these below run in Positron’s terminal exactly like Claude Code does, and Gemini CLI is free with an ordinary Google account, though you can quickly run out of tokens using the free tier. The underlying skills we will cover (directing an agent, verifying its output) transfer. Just know that in-class instruction, troubleshooting help, and these materials will all assume Claude Code, so you’re on your own for translating anything tool-specific.

Gemini CLI: Google’s coding agent for the terminal. The closest free stand-in for Claude Code, and the one to pick if you would rather not pay. Free with a Google account.
Codex: OpenAI’s coding agent for the terminal. A good fit if you already pay for ChatGPT and want to stay in that account. Needs a paid ChatGPT plan.

title: Software & Setup
section: Set up later in the semester
text:
Set up later in the semester
You don’t need these before the first class. We’ll set them up together when we get to them.

A Gemini API key (Week 7). We’ll use it to have your agent generate images with Google’s image model (Nano Banana). It’s paid per image (see AI Tools and Cost). We’ll also cover how to keep the key secret: it never goes in your code or in a commit.
Python packages. Each build has its own project folder, and your agent installs the packages that project needs with uv add (for example, Pillow for images or plotnine for charts). You don’t need to install them ahead of time.
Quarto with Python. When a Quarto document runs Python code, the project needs ipykernel installed, and Quarto has to use that project’s Python. The simplest way is to run Quarto through uv:
uv add ipykernel
uv run quarto render
We write Python in .py scripts and .qmd files. We don’t use Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) in this course.

That’s it - you’re all set for class!
